Chinmay, you keep saying you want to leave the bank and cook for a living. Let your Karthik mama tell you what I did at your age.

I was twenty-five, an insurance clerk, and I dreamed of a restaurant. My friend Lalitha ran a small mess in Mylapore. I asked if I could work her kitchen on Sundays, no pay. For six months I chopped onions, burnt rice, washed pots.

Here is what I learned. I hated the dinner rush. I loved the early mornings, the dough, the ovens. Lalitha said, "You're not a cook, you're a baker."

So I kept my job one more year and took a baking course in the evenings. Only then did I leave. The bakery is thirty years old now. If I had quit that first month, I'd have opened the wrong shop.

qa.a: Lalitha ran a small mess in Mylapore.

qa.a: He felt genuinely happy and absorbed with the dough and ovens, unlike the dinner rush, which he hated.

qa.q: How might Lalitha have seen Karthik in her kitchen?
qa.a: Lalitha probably saw an eager but clumsy helper and noticed which tasks lit him up, which is why she could tell him he was a baker.

Abhinav had exactly fifteen minutes. Jasleen, a product designer at a startup two floors up, had agreed to meet him in the lobby between her calls.

"So you're an accountant who wants to do design?" she said, sitting down with her coffee.

"I think so. I've done a free online course. Nights, mostly." He opened his laptop to show the app screens he'd made for his building's water-tank schedule.

Jasleen scrolled. "These are messy. But you solved a real problem." She pointed. "The course won't teach you this part: talking to users. Ask your neighbours to try it and watch where they get stuck."

Her phone buzzed. She stood. "Do that for a month. Then message me."

Abhinav stayed in the lobby another ten minutes, writing down every word she'd said, heart still thumping.

On Saturday mornings, Vijay now takes the 9:15 bus to a learning centre in Shivajinagar instead of sleeping till noon.

It started after he told Dolma, the centre's coordinator, that he'd always wanted to teach but was stuck doing audits. She didn't tell him to quit. She said, "Take the Class 6 maths group for two months. See how you feel."

The first Saturday was chaos. Twelve kids, one broken marker, and a boy who asked why fractions existed at all. Vijay went home tired and oddly light.

By the fifth week he'd made fraction cards from cereal boxes. Dolma watched from the door. "They listen to you," she said. "But you're still slow with the quiet ones."

Vijay wrote that down too. At his audit desk on Monday he hummed, and a colleague asked what had happened.

The bench by the harbour in Cape Town was cold, and Tariq had his hands deep in his jacket.

"My cousin just made partner at a law firm," he said. "He's twenty-seven."

Zanele laughed softly. "I started nursing at thirty-one. Before that I cleaned offices for eight years."

"Do you ever feel late?"

"All the time, at first. Then I noticed the people I admired most had strange, crooked roads."

Tariq was quiet. He was twenty-six, three years into a job he half liked, and he'd started a night course in marine biology. At his pace it would take four years.

"Four years is fine," Zanele said. "Ask whether you're closer to the person you want to be. Not closer to your cousin."

He watched a fishing boat come in slowly. For the first time that week, slow didn't sound like failure.

The evening college library smelt of old paper and floor polish. Chandrika, twenty-five, sat at the long table with a blank page and a pencil.

Rekha, who sat beside her in accounts class and was forty-four, peered over. "Planning your wedding?"

"Planning five years." Chandrika wrote a line across the top: 2025 to 2030. "Everyone from school already has everything. I kept making one-month plans and hating myself on the first of every month."

"And now?"

"Now I'm trying this." Under 2025: finish the diploma. 2026: move to a proper accounts job. 2027: maybe my own flat. Beside each year she wrote one word: honest, steady, independent.

Rekha tapped the page. "I got my first real job at thirty-nine. Nobody gave me a medal for being late, and nobody took one away either."

Chandrika laughed, and kept writing.

qa.q: How old was Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha was forty-four.

qa.q: How can you tell Chandrika felt calmer with the five-year plan?
qa.a: She laughed and kept writing, instead of hating herself as she had on the first of every month with her one-month plans.

qa.q: Why might the words beside each year help Chandrika?
qa.a: Words like honest, steady and independent let her measure progress by what she values, not by what her schoolmates already have.

qa.q: If you were Rekha, what would you want Chandrika to take from your story?
qa.a: You would want her to see that late starts are normal and that her path is worth walking at her own pace.

Dear Rukmini,

You asked in your last letter how I stopped panicking about being "so behind." I don't think I stopped completely. But it's quieter, so here's what I did.

I threw away the timeline I'd built in college: job at 22, flat at 24, married at 26. I'm 26 and I have none of those in that order.

Instead I made a list of what I actually care about: doing careful work, being near Amma as she gets older, playing the tabla. Every few months I check if my days look more like that. Mostly, slowly, they do.

I also started collecting stories. Our old principal became a teacher at 38. My neighbour opened her tailoring shop at 50.

You're only 23. Your road is allowed to bend.

With love,
Tushar

Vera's first week in Vienna felt like a film she'd been dropped into.

She rode the tram just to ride it. She bought a pastry every morning from a different bakery and rated them in a notebook. She signed up for the climbing club, the choir and a Tuesday language exchange, all on the same afternoon.

"You're like a tourist who lives here," said Ivan, her new flatmate, watching her unpack a fourth second-hand lamp.

"Everything's new!" Vera said. "Even the light switches."

Her mother called twice on Wednesday. Vera texted, "Can't talk, at the museum, love you!!" and felt a small twist she ignored.

That night she lay on her mattress listening to the trams and was too excited to sleep. Novi Sad felt a thousand kilometres away. It was, roughly. She didn't mind at all.

"There's a dosa counter AND a pasta counter," she whispered to Asif, who was also nineteen and also from a small town. "And the hostel room has a window facing a lake!"

The days ran together happily. Badminton at seven, sessions till five, biryani with the other trainees at night. She joined the dance club and the quiz team. When her father called, she talked so fast about the lake that he laughed and gave up asking whether she was eating properly.

Only once, on Thursday, did she notice she hadn't thought of home all day. She felt oddly proud, then oddly hollow, then someone knocked on the door for night badminton and she forgot it.

By the second week in Chennai, Yamini had a list on her phone titled Things That Are Wrong.

The broker wanted two months' rent as commission. The flat's tap coughed brown water every morning. The bank needed a local address proof, but the rental agreement needed a bank account. At the corner mess everything came with rice, and the rasam made her eyes stream.

"In Lucknow," she began, at dinner.

"I know," said Reena, her roommate from Ranchi, "In Lucknow the rotis are softer. You said."

Yamini laughed, but it came out sharp. On the auto home she'd tried asking for the market in her few words of Tamil, and the driver had answered in rapid Tamil and then shrugged. She had wanted to cry at a shrug.

That night she added: Autos. Rasam. Myself.

I'm Tejas. By my third week in Delhi, I'd started keeping score, and Delhi was losing.

In Kolhapur, water came when you opened a tap. Here, it came at 5 a.m. and not always then. In Kolhapur, a rickshaw driver knew your father. Here, I paid double twice before I learned to argue. The mess dal tasted of nothing. My hostel form was rejected because I'd signed in blue ink instead of black.

I remember sitting on my trunk, holding the rejected form, and wanting to throw my phone across the room.

Baljeet, the senior in the next room, knocked. "Black pen?" He handed me one. "Everyone gets rejected once. It's like a welcome."

I laughed, a little. I still thought Delhi was worse. But it had given me a pen.

Lokesh, you asked why I went quiet in October. Okay. I'm Pooja, I'm from Jorhat, and for about three weeks I cried every night in the hostel bathroom with the tap running so nobody would hear.

Nothing bad happened. That was the strange part. Classes were fine. But nobody here knew me. At home, the man at the tea stall knows how I take my tea. Here I was just "the northeast girl" and people asked if I ate snakes, which, no.

I missed Ma's fish tenga so badly I actually dreamt about it. I looked at train tickets home twice. I didn't buy them.

What I figured out, slowly, is that wanting to go home didn't mean coming here was a mistake. It meant I'd left something real behind. Both things were true at once.

Tejas, beta, you sound like I did in 1994. Sit, let me tell you.

I came to Mumbai from Indore at nineteen for my hotel management course. Everyone here spoke fast, walked fast, ate fast. My roommate was from Goa and put vinegar in things. I didn't know one person who remembered my birthday.

The first month I was fine. The second month I cried every night into my dupatta so my roommate wouldn't hear. I wrote to my mother, "I want to come back." I posted it and then regretted it.

She wrote back: "Come if you need to. Your room is here. But give it till Diwali."

I gave it till Diwali. And your Alka aunty is still here, thirty years later. The crying didn't mean I was wrong to come. It meant I was far from everything that knew me.

The power went out in Shillong just as Elizabeth dialled her son. The phone had eight per cent battery.

"Mama?" Kamal's voice from Pune was flat. "I'm fine. Just tired."

Elizabeth had heard that flatness three calls in a row. Her chest tightened. The old words rose up: Come home, this was a mistake, who told you to go so far. She held them.

"Tired how?" she asked instead, watching the candle.

"Nobody here says my name right. The food is... I don't know, Mama."

"I miss you too," she said. "Your chair looks very empty." Then, carefully: "Tell me one thing that wasn't bad today."

A pause. "The college canteen had momos. Terrible momos."

She laughed. The battery flashed red. "Sunday, same time? I'll charge the phone."

"Sunday," he said, and he sounded a little less tired.

qa.q: How much battery did Elizabeth's phone have?
qa.a: The phone had eight per cent battery.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she heard the flatness in Kamal's voice?

In the Kochi flat, Francis set two cups of tea on the table out of habit before remembering that Tushar was in Delhi.

Their Sunday call came at eight, as always. Tushar's face on the screen looked thinner.

"Hostel food," he said, when Francis asked. "It's fine, Pappa."

Francis heard what wasn't fine. His hand went to the second cup. He wanted to say, Your mother cried twice this week. You don't have to stay there. Instead he said, "The mango tree has fruit. Mummy is making pickle. I'll courier a jar."

Tushar smiled for the first time. "The spicy one?"

"The spicy one."

After the call, Francis stayed at the table for a long time. The empty chair was hard. But Tushar had laughed, and a jar of pickle was something he could actually do.

Sunday, 8 p.m.

Four months in Hyderabad and my weekends are still silent.

At work everyone is nice. Sabina shares her tiffin, asks how I'm settling. But at 6 p.m. everyone goes home to their own people, and on Saturday nobody texts.

This month I tried things:
1. The running club at the lake. Went twice. Everyone had their own group. I ran alone next to them.
2. Said hi to the family next door. The aunty gave me murukku. Then the door closed.
3. The Kerala association Onam lunch. That one was nice. A woman from Thrissur talked about her mother's pickles for twenty minutes.

I keep thinking I'm failing at this. But I read somewhere that real friendships take a lot of hours. I've had maybe six.

Next Saturday: running club again. And I'll ask the Thrissur woman for her number.

Kalyani

The hospital in Nimbahera closed its outpatient wing at two, and after that Elizabeth, twenty-four and newly posted from Kottayam, had nothing but a quiet room above a grocery shop.

The doctors were polite. The other nurses were friendly in the corridor and spoke Mewari to each other at lunch, laughing at things she half caught.

Her landlady, Kalyani-bai, invited her to the Ganesh temple on Tuesday. Elizabeth went, stood at the back, and was handed prasad by six strangers.

On Sunday she found the only other Malayali in town, a bank clerk, through a notice in the church. They talked for an hour about rain.

Walking back past the shuttered market, Elizabeth counted: two months, one bank clerk, a landlady who waved. It felt small. But on Tuesday she'd go to the temple again.

qa.q: What time did the outpatient wing close?
qa.a: It closed at two.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling as she walked back past the shuttered market?
qa.a: She felt lonely and a little discouraged that two months had given her so few connections, yet still hopeful enough to keep trying.

qa.q: How could a colleague support Elizabeth at this stage?
qa.a: A nurse could include her in lunch by switching to a language she knows, or invite her along on a day off.

qa.q: How might Kalyani-bai see her new tenant?
qa.a: Kalyani-bai seems to see a quiet young woman far from home and wants to include her, which is why she invited her to the temple.

grounding: In a small town, a young nurse finds colleagues friendly but distant and tries temple, landlady and a regional contact, learning friendship is slow.

Monday: Maria's fever started at the office. By evening in her new Hyderabad flat, she was shivering under two blankets with nobody to ask for water. She went to the clinic nearby and came back with medicine and a strange loneliness.

Wednesday: Still weak, she opened her laptop and found an email: the client had rejected her whole proposal. She sat on the kitchen floor and thought, why did I leave Goa? Everyone I know is there. She typed a resignation note and saved it.

Friday: Almost without deciding to, she messaged Disha, a teammate she'd had lunch with twice: "Sorry to bother you. I'm sick and it's been a bad week." Twenty minutes later Disha replied: "Coming with khichdi. Address?"

That evening they sat on the floor and ate. Maria laughed for the first time all week, and deleted the resignation draft.

qa.q: What did Disha bring?
qa.a: Disha came with khichdi.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling on the kitchen floor on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt defeated and full of doubt about the move, sick and alone, and even typed a resignation note.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage, and how did Maria use it?
qa.a: Reaching out to someone nearby; Maria's message to Disha brought company and food, which made the week feel survivable.

qa.q: What is it like for Disha to get Maria's message?
qa.a: Disha likely felt concerned and glad to be asked, responding quickly and warmly to a newer teammate.

grounding: Across one bad week, illness and a work setback in a new city feel much worse alone until reaching out to someone turns it.

Vandana, sit. You asked if I ever regretted leaving Bhopal. Let your Pranav mama tell you about one week.

I was twenty-four, new in Kolkata, a junior at a shipping firm. In my third month, it rained for four days straight. My room flooded, my shoes rotted, and I got a fever. Then my manager told me I'd made a mistake in a report, in front of everyone.

That Friday I sat on my bed with my feet in water and thought, I'll take the Sunday train home and never come back.

Instead, for no reason, I called Subrata, a quiet clerk from my office. I said, "My room is flooded." He came in an hour with a bucket and a flask of tea.

We're still friends. That call was the whole turning point, beta. Not the job, not the city. One phone call.

qa.a: He came with a bucket and a flask of tea.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling that Friday on the bed with his feet in water?
qa.a: He felt defeated and alone, doubting the move so much that he planned to go home for good.

qa.q: What was the choice inside the story that changed things?
qa.a: Calling Subrata, a quiet colleague, and admitting he was struggling; that one call brought help and a lasting friendship.

qa.q: How might Subrata have felt when Pranav called?
qa.a: Subrata may have been surprised but glad to be trusted, and he felt enough care to come at once with help.

grounding: An elder recalls a low week in a new city, where illness and a work setback deepened doubt until reaching out turned it.

Madhuri's laptop was stolen from the Guwahati bus on Tuesday, two days before her project deadline, and the new city felt suddenly hostile.

She filed a report at the police station, then sat in a café with a cold coffee and no backup of her last week's work. She had no family here. Her friends were in Nagpur. The office knew her as the quiet new analyst.

The doubt came hard: What am I even doing here?

Her phone showed one name from the office she'd chatted with: Naveen, who had helped her find the canteen on day one. She almost didn't. Then she typed: "My laptop got stolen and I'm a bit lost. Do you know how IT handles this?"

He called back within minutes, walked her through the IT steps, and said, "Come in early tomorrow. We'll rebuild the slides together."

She paid for the coffee and, for the first time that day, breathed out.

qa.q: Where was Madhuri's laptop stolen?
qa.a: It was stolen from the Guwahati bus.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling in the café?
qa.a: She felt alone and overwhelmed, doubting her move to the city with no support nearby and a deadline looming.

qa.q: Which choice turned Madhuri's day, and why?
qa.a: Messaging Naveen despite barely knowing him; asking for help brought practical support and a small sense of belonging.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Madhuri's message?
qa.a: Naveen seems to see a new colleague in real trouble and wants to help, glad she thought of him.

grounding: With a stolen laptop and a deadline in an unfamiliar city, doubt peaks until reaching out to a colleague changes the stretch.

Six months after moving from Ludhiana to Chennai, Neelam had a Saturday that almost looked like a life.

At seven she walked to the same corner stall for filter coffee. The owner now poured it without asking and scolded her in Tamil for skipping last week. She answered, badly, in Tamil, and he laughed.

At ten she went to the yoga class near the beach, where she knew three names now.

In the evening she took the bus to the gurdwara in T. Nagar, as she'd done every Sunday at home with her grandmother. There she met Gurpreet, who ran a bakery in Anna Nagar and asked if she wanted to help with the langar next month.

Back in her flat, Neelam lit the small diya her mother had packed, and ate curd rice. Both things felt right.

qa.a: She took the bus to the gurdwara in T. Nagar.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling as she lit the diya and ate curd rice?
qa.a: She felt settled and content, with both her home ritual and her new habits feeling right together.

qa.q: What small step could deepen Neelam's roots further?

"Same as usual?" Chandrika asked from behind the counter.

"Same as usual," said Omkar, and felt oddly pleased that there was a usual.

"Two months now," she said, pouring the coffee. "You came in the first week looking like someone had stolen your dog."

When I first came to Dubai for the engineering job, my weekends were a hole. I'm Pranav, and I lasted about two months of sleeping till noon and scrolling before I decided to build something like a week.

I found a small cricket club that played on Friday mornings in a dusty ground near Al Quoz. I found a Kerala restaurant where the owner started saving me the last parotta. I learned to say thank you in Arabic and started saying it to the watchman every morning.

Some things I brought with me. Every Sunday night I call my grandmother, and I still light an agarbatti by the window before work, the way we did at home.

Joseph, my flatmate from Manila, laughed at the agarbatti at first. Now he asks for one when he has an exam. The week has a shape. That shape holds me up.

The transport strike began the morning Reena started her new job, so Madhav walked her from the metro to the office, forty minutes in the Kolkata heat.

A year earlier, he'd been the one lost. He'd cried in his rented room in Salt Lake and nearly gone back to Nagpur. Now he knew which lanes had shade, which tea stall had clean cups, and how to say "a little less sugar" in Bangla.

"How do you know all this?" Reena asked, sweating.

"I didn't, once. I'll text you a list tonight. Where to buy a gas cylinder. A doctor who speaks Hindi. A good mutton roll."

"Do you miss Nagpur?"

"Every day. And I'd miss this place if I left." Madhav said it and realised it was true. He called his mother every Sunday; he also knew the neighbourhood tailor by name. Both felt like home.

qa.q: Where had Madhav rented his room a year earlier?
qa.a: He rented a room in Salt Lake.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he realised he'd miss Kolkata too?
qa.a: He felt a quiet surprise and gratitude, recognising that both cities now felt like home.

qa.q: What could Madhav keep doing to help Reena through the next months?
qa.a: He could send the promised list and check in on her during the hard early weeks, since he knows that stage well.

qa.q: What is it like for Reena to be guided on her first day during the strike?
qa.a: Reena is hot and tired but likely relieved and grateful to have someone who knows the city walk with her.

grounding: During a strike, a person who settled over a year helps a newcomer, holding gratitude and ties to two homes.

On his fourteenth month in Mumbai, Sumit noticed he'd stopped calling the flat in Andheri "the room" and started calling it home.

It happened the day Hansa joined his team from Jaipur. She sat at her desk with a stiff smile and the same lost look he remembered in his own mirror.

At lunch he took her to the Gujarati thali place he'd found after weeks of searching. He told her which local train to avoid at nine. He gave her the number of his building's cook.

"Do you still miss Patna?" Hansa asked.

"On Chhath, a lot," Sumit said. "I go home for it every year. But when I land back here, I feel relieved too."

That night he messaged his mother a photo of the monsoon from his window: "Thank you for letting me go." And then, to Hansa: "Monsoon tip: carry two umbrellas."

qa.q: Which month in Mumbai was Sumit in when he started calling the flat home?
qa.a: It was his fourteenth month in Mumbai.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when he messaged his mother?
qa.a: He felt grateful, both for Mumbai and for his mother letting him leave Patna.

qa.q: How could Sumit keep helping Hansa over the next weeks?
qa.a: He could keep sharing small practical tips and invite her to regular lunches, since he remembers how lost the first months feel.

qa.q: How might Hansa see Sumit on her first days?
qa.a: Hansa probably sees him as a relief, a colleague who understands being new and makes the city less overwhelming.

grounding: After more than a year, a person feels at home in two places, is grateful and helps a newcomer through the same path.
